body_text:
Good morning,

Here's what's moving in startup land today.

TOP STORY: AI infrastructure funding surges past $8B in H1 2026
Venture funding into AI infrastructure and observability tooling crossed $8.1B in the first half of 2026, up 64% year over year, driven by a wave of Series A and B rounds as enterprises move AI workloads from pilot to production. Investors we spoke to point to rising operational complexity — and the cost of downtime in production AI systems — as the driver behind renewed interest in monitoring and observability plays.

ALSO TODAY:

- A Boston-based warehouse robotics company closed a $40M Series B led by a new industrial-focused fund, its first outside round in two years.

- Three enterprise SaaS companies announced layoffs this week totaling roughly 400 roles, as boards push harder on default-alive timelines heading into Q4 budget season.

- A wave of Series A companies are reporting longer diligence periods on SOC 2 and security reviews before enterprise contracts close, according to a survey of 200 B2B SaaS founders released this morning — average time from LOI to signed contract is now 11 weeks, up from 7 weeks two years ago.

- Y Combinator's latest batch demo day drew record attendance from corporate VC arms, with several strategics reportedly writing first checks directly off demo day pitches.

- A well-known observability incumbent quietly raised prices on its usage-based tiers for the second time this year, prompting a wave of complaints on social media from customers who say their bills doubled without a corresponding jump in usage. Several smaller challengers in the space have started running ad campaigns directly referencing the price hike, betting that migration friction is lower than the incumbent assumes.

- A survey of 150 VCs released this morning found that 71% expect Series A round sizes to grow modestly in H2 2026, reversing the flat-to-down trend of the last two years, as capital deployment picks back up across growth-stage funds flush with fresh commitments.

FUNDING ROUNDUP: 14 rounds closed yesterday totaling $612M across seed through Series C. The largest was a $95M Series C for a logistics-software company; the smallest was a $2.5M pre-seed for a two-person team building tooling for AI agent evaluation. Full list on the site.

ONE MORE THING: We're tracking a growing number of Series A companies bringing on a part-time or fractional CFO in the 6-12 months after closing, rather than waiting for a Series B to make the hire full-time — worth a longer piece if there's reader interest, reply and let us know.

That's it for today — see you tomorrow.

— The TechCrunch AM Team

subject: How the best Series A founders run their board meetings
snippet: Hi all, I've sat in on a lot of board meetings over the years, both as an operator and later as an advisor, and the gap between a board meeting that builds trust and one that burns
body_text:
Hi all,

I've sat in on a lot of board meetings over the years, both as an operator and later as an advisor, and the gap between a board meeting that builds trust and one that burns it usually comes down to a handful of habits. Here's what I've seen work.

1. Send the deck 48-72 hours ahead, not the night before.
This sounds obvious, but I'd guess fewer than half of Series A founders actually do it consistently. A deck that arrives the night before gets skimmed in the car on the way to the meeting. A deck that arrives three days early gets read twice, and board members show up with real questions instead of surface-level ones. The best founders I know treat the pre-read as more important than the meeting itself.

2. Lead with the bad news, not the good news.
Every founder wants to open with the win of the quarter. Don't. Open with what's off track — a slipping enterprise deal, a metric that missed plan, a hire who didn't work out — and frame it before anyone else can. Boards that hear bad news from the founder first trust the founder more, not less. Boards that discover it themselves, or hear it buried on slide 14, start wondering what else isn't being said.

3. Bring one real decision, not ten status updates.
Most board decks are 80% reporting and 20% decision-making, and it should be closer to the reverse. Pick the one or two decisions that actually need the board's input — a pricing change, a key hire, a runway-extending trade-off — and spend most of the meeting there. Status updates can live in an async pre-read.

4. Get ahead of the number that's about to change.
If a metric is about to move in a way that will surprise the board next quarter — a big customer churning, a renewal slipping, a cost line jumping — flag it this quarter, even directionally. Nothing erodes trust faster than a board member feeling blindsided by something the founder clearly saw coming.

5. End with a specific ask.
Don't let the meeting end on 'any questions?' End with 'here's what I need from each of you before we talk next' — an intro, a decision, a gut check on a hire. Boards that leave with a job to do stay engaged between meetings. Boards that leave with nothing to do drift.

If you're prepping for a board meeting in the next few weeks, I'd genuinely love to hear which of these lands hardest for you — reply and let me know.

— Lenny
body_html:
Lenny's Newsletter

How the best Series A founders run their board meetings

Five habits: send the deck 48–72 hours early, lead with bad news, bring one real decision instead of ten status updates, flag the metric about to move, and end with a specific ask.

Read the full essay →

subject: Crunchbase Daily: A $2.1B week for AI infrastructure startups
snippet: Good morning, Here's what closed this week. BIG ROUND: An AI observability startup out of Seattle closed a $180M Series C at a $2.4B valuation, led by a growth-stage fund making it
body_text:
Good morning,

Here's what closed this week.

BIG ROUND: An AI observability startup out of Seattle closed a $180M Series C at a $2.4B valuation, led by a growth-stage fund making its first bet in the category. The round brings the company's total raised to $340M since its 2022 seed.

SERIES A/B ROUNDUP:
- A developer tools startup building CI/CD for AI pipelines raised a $22M Series A.
- A fintech infrastructure company closed a $45M Series B, its second round in 14 months.
- A supply chain visibility platform raised a $31M Series A led by a logistics-focused fund.
- An API security startup closed an $18M Series A, its first institutional round after two years bootstrapped.

TOTAL FOR THE WEEK: $2.1B across 34 announced rounds in infrastructure and dev tools, the highest weekly total in the category since March.

WHAT WE'RE WATCHING: Several investors we track are flagging that Series A infra rounds are increasingly conditioned on customer concentration — boards want to see revenue spread across at least 3-4 meaningful accounts before a B round, not one large logo carrying the metrics.

ACQUISITIONS: A monitoring startup was acquired by a larger observability platform for an undisclosed sum, its third acquisition in the space this year. A separate deal saw a log-management vendor absorbed into a larger security suite, part of a broader trend of point-solution observability tools consolidating under bigger platform plays as customers push back on tool sprawl.

VALUATIONS: Median Series A pre-money valuation for infrastructure and dev-tools companies ticked up to $42M this quarter, from $38M last quarter, though still below the 2024 peak of $58M. Investors we spoke with attribute the modest recovery to stronger enterprise pull-through on AI-adjacent tooling rather than a broad re-rating of the category.

PEOPLE MOVES: A former VP Engineering at a well-known observability unicorn joined a growth-stage fund as an operating partner focused on infrastructure investments — the third such hire among major funds this year, a sign that firms are leaning harder on operator diligence before writing infra checks.

WHAT'S NEXT: Several bankers we track expect the fall to bring a wave of Series B processes for companies that raised Series A rounds in late 2024 and early 2025, as those cohorts hit the 18-24 month mark that typically triggers the next fundraising cycle.

That's the week — see you tomorrow.

— Crunchbase Daily

subject: SaaStr Annual 2026 — Speaker Portal Access + Slide Deck Deadline (Aug 25)
snippet: Hi Maya, We're thrilled to confirm your session at SaaStr Annual 2026. Here's everything you need for the next few weeks. YOUR SESSION Title: 'Scaling Observability Trust With Ente
body_text:
Hi Maya,

We're thrilled to confirm your session at SaaStr Annual 2026. Here's everything you need for the next few weeks.

YOUR SESSION
Title: 'Scaling Observability Trust With Enterprise Customers'
Date/Time: Tuesday, September 22, 2:15pm-2:45pm PT
Room: Cloud Stage B, San Mateo Event Center
Format: Solo talk with 10 minutes of Q&A

WHAT WE NEED FROM YOU
1. Slide deck (16:9, PDF or PPTX) — due August 25. Our AV team needs lead time to load decks onto the venue systems and do a tech check.
2. Updated headshot and 100-word bio — due August 25, same deadline as the deck. This goes on the event app and printed signage.
3. A one-sentence session abstract for the printed program, if you'd like to revise the one submitted at CFP time — optional, due August 25 if you want changes.

SPEAKER PORTAL
You can upload all of the above directly through the speaker portal: portal.saastr.com/speakers (login: the email this was sent to). The portal also has your green room access code and a map of backstage entrances for Cloud Stage B.

DAY-OF LOGISTICS
Please arrive at the green room by 1:30pm for a mic check and a quick run-through with our stage manager. Green room access is through the west loading dock — your badge will be flagged for speaker access at registration.

We'll also need a $0 W-9 on file for our records even though this is an unpaid speaking slot, standard for our vendor system — the portal has a template if you don't have one handy.

HOTEL AND TRAVEL
We've held a small block of rooms at the San Mateo Marriott (0.4 miles from the venue) at the conference rate of $289/night for speakers, available through August 30 or until the block sells out, whichever comes first. The booking link is also in the speaker portal under 'Travel.' Flights and ground transport are on you, but the portal has a list of discounted rideshare codes valid for the event week.

OTHER SESSIONS YOU MIGHT WANT TO CATCH
If you're arriving the day before, Monday afternoon has a track on Series A-to-B fundraising dynamics that a few other speakers flagged as worth attending, and there's a speakers-only dinner Monday night at 7pm if you'd like to meet the rest of the Cloud Stage B lineup beforehand — RSVP through the portal if you can make it.

PRESS AND RECORDING
Your session will be recorded and posted to the SaaStr YouTube channel within two weeks of the event, and a few press outlets typically sit in on Cloud Stage sessions — let us know in the portal if there's anything you'd prefer to keep off the record.

Let us know if anything above needs adjusting, and congratulations again on being selected — this track had over 400 submissions this year.

Best,
The SaaStr Speaker Relations Team

Deck, headshot, and bio all due August 25 via the speaker portal.
